claim: Breast cancer is the most common cancer worldwide, with 2.3 million cases diagnosed and 685,000 deaths in 2020.
source: Breast cancer is the most common cancer worldwide, with 2.3 million cases diagnosed and 685,000 deaths in 2020 (WHO, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2021 report

claim: Early detection and diagnosis from screening may reduce mortality by up to 65% among breast cancer patients.
source: Early detection and diagnosis from screening may reduce mortality by up to 65% among breast cancer patients (Berry et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Berry et al., 2005

claim: Populations with a good uptake rate in screening programs can achieve a 90% 5-year survival rate in patients who received an early diagnosis attributed to screening.
source: Populations with a good uptake rate in screening programs can achieve a 90% 5-year survival rate in patients who received an early diagnosis attributed to screening (WHO, 2021).

claim: The initial search retrieved 1207 articles and 935 independent records.
source: The initial search retrieved 1207 articles and 935 independent records.
evidence: Direct statement of search results from the study methodology

claim: After screening, 26 cross-sectional studies from 13 countries were eligible for inclusion.
source: After screening (see 'Methods'), 26 cross-sectional studies from 13 countries were eligible for inclusion (Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement of included studies with reference to Table 1

claim: 7 reports came from Europe.
source: In total, 7 reports came from Europe (Campbell et al., 2021; Jidkova et al., 2022; Knoll et al., 2022; Eijkelboom et al., 2021; Losurdo et al., 2022; Toss et al., 2021; NHS England, 2021)
evidence: Direct count of studies from Europe with citations

claim: 2 reports came from Oceania.
source: 2 from Oceania (BreastScreen Australia, 2020; BreastScreen Aoteroa, 2022)
evidence: Direct count of studies from Oceania with citations

claim: 1 report came from Asia.
source: 1 from Asia (Shen et al., 2022)
evidence: Direct count of studies from Asia with citation

claim: 2 reports came from South America.
source: 2 from South America (Bessa, 2021; Ribeiro et al., 2022)
evidence: Direct count of studies from South America with citations

claim: 14 reports came from North America.
source: 14 from North America (Chiarelli et al., 2021; Walker et al., 2021; Doubova et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021; Amornsiripanitch et al., 2021; Becker et al., 2021; DeGroff et al., 2021; Dennis et al., 2021; Fedewa et al., 2021; Lehman et al., 2022; London et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2021; Sprague et al., 2021; Nyante et al., 2021).
evidence: Direct count of studies from North America with citations

claim: The most frequently reported country was the USA (n = 11).
source: The most frequently reported country was the USA (n = 11).

claim: Studies examined either regional (n = 13) or national populations (n = 13).
source: Studies examined either regional (n = 13) or national populations (n = 13).
evidence: Direct count of study population types

claim: All 13 countries/nations had international movement controls in place.
source: Table 1 shows that all 13 countries/nations had international movement controls in place
evidence: Data from Table 1 showing restriction types

claim: 23 study-specific regions had internal movement controls.
source: 23 study-specific regions had internal movement controls

claim: 21 study-specific regions had stay-at home requirements in place.
source: 21 study-specific regions had stay-at home requirements in place

claim: 1 study-specific region (Northern Italy, Emilia Romagna) had public transport closures.
source: 1 study-specific region (Northern Italy, Emilia Romagna) had public transport closures

claim: 23 study-specific regions had bans on gatherings >10 people.
source: 23 study-specific regions had bans on gatherings >10 people

claim: 24 study-specific regions had public events bans in place.
source: 24 study-specific regions had public events bans in place

claim: 24 study-specific regions had workplace closures in place.
source: 24 study-specific regions had workplace closures in place

claim: 23 study-specific regions had in-person school closures in place.
source: 23 study-specific regions had in-person school closures in place (Mathieu, 2022; CIHI, 2022; Commonwealth of Massachusetts, 2021; Commonwealth of Virginia, 2023; Cooper et al., 2023; SPICe, 2023; State of Michigan, 2020; State of North Carolina, 2020).
evidence: Count from Table 1 data with supporting citations

claim: Summary data from 17 studies in eight countries reporting breast cancer screening volumes, and data from 106,484,908 women before and after COVID-19 infection control measures were extracted.
source: Summary data from 17 studies in eight countries reporting breast cancer screening volumes, and data from 106,484,908 women before and after COVID-19 infection control measures were extracted (data from 2017 to 2020 were the comparison time period, Table 2; Doubova et al., 2021; Bessa, 2021; Ribeiro et al., 2022; Chiarelli et al., 2021; Losurdo et al., 2022; Walker et al., 2021; NHS England, 2021; Shen et al., 2022; BreastScreen Australia, 2020; DeGroff et al., 2021; Lehman et al., 2022; Amornsiripanitch et al., 2021; Sprague et al., 2021; London et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2021; Nyante et al., 2021; Becker et al., 2021).
evidence: Direct statement of data extraction with citations

claim: In countries with national screening programs, a negative change in screening volume was reported.
source: In countries with national screening programs, a negative change in screening volume was reported
evidence: Summary statement based on data from multiple studies

claim: The lowest volume change in countries with national screening programs was estimated at –12.86% in Australia.
source: with the lowest volume change estimated at –12.86% in Australia (BreastScreen Australia, 2020)

claim: England had a –15.80% change in screening volume.
source: followed by –15.80% in England (NHS England, 2021).

claim: Brazil had a –41.49% change in screening volume.
source: A larger negative change in screening volume was observed in Brazil (–41.49%) (Ribeiro et al., 2022)

claim: Mexico had a –61.30% change in screening volume.
source: and Mexico (–61.30%) (Doubova et al., 2021).

claim: Brazil has coverage of ~24% of the eligible population for breast screening.
source: Brazil having coverage of ~24% and Mexico having ~20% coverage of the eligible population (OECD, 2021a; Unger-Saldaña et al., 2020).

claim: Mexico has ~20% coverage of the eligible population for breast screening.
source: Brazil having coverage of ~24% and Mexico having ~20% coverage of the eligible population (OECD, 2021a; Unger-Saldaña et al., 2020).

claim: A significant proportion of breast screening in Brazil and Mexico consists of opportunistic screening programs.
source: A significant proportion of breast screening in Brazil and Mexico consists of opportunistic screening programs.
evidence: Direct statement based on healthcare system characteristics

claim: Using data from Health Managed Organization (HMO) Blue Cross Blue Shield (BCBS) from the state of Michigan, the authors observed an 18.10% overall increase in screening volume.
source: Using data from Health Managed Organization (HMO) Blue Cross Blue Shield (BCBS) from the state of Michigan, the authors observed temporal changes in rates with an increase slightly above 2019 levels in the last few months of 2020, with an 18.10% overall increase in screening volume (Becker et al., 2021).

claim: The odds that a woman received breast cancer screening remained 20% lower in 2020 relative to 2019 in the Michigan HMO study.
source: Although rates were above 2019 levels, the authors noted that the odds that a woman received breast cancer screening remained 20% lower in 2020 relative to 2019 (Becker et al., 2021).

claim: Six studies with data among populations wholly or partially covered by national insurance showed a decrease in screening volume.
source: This was consistent with the decrease in screening volume that was generally observed from six studies with data among populations wholly or partially covered by national insurance (Lehman et al., 2022; Amornsiripanitch et al., 2021; Sprague et al., 2021; London et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2021; Nyante et al., 2021).
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple studies with citations

claim: Percentage decreases in screening volume among populations with national insurance ranged from –36.50 to –9.80%.
source: Percentage decreases ranged from –36.50 (Lehman et al., 2022) to –9.80% (Miller et al., 2021).

claim: The USA National Breast and Cervical Cancer Early Detection Program (NBCCEDP) reported a –39.00% decrease in volume.
source: Data from the USA National Breast and Cervical Cancer Early Detection Program (NBCCEDP), which provides cancer screening services to women with low income and inadequate health insurance, reported a greater decrease (–39.00%) in volume (DeGroff et al., 2021).
evidence: Specific data point with citation and program description

claim: In the USA, where there is a mix of national (Medicare) and private insurance depending on age, screening volume changes were similar to other national screening programs at –36.50%.
source: In the USA, where there is a mix of national (Medicare) and private insurance depending on age, screening volume changes were similar to other national screening programs at –36.50% (Lehman et al., 2022).
evidence: Specific data point with citation and context

claim: A positive increase in volume of +30% was observed among private insurance providers in the USA.
source: In contrast, a positive increase in volume was observed among private insurance providers +30% (London et al., 2022).

claim: A total of nine cross-sectional studies reported breast cancer screening participation rates and represented >46,257,402 participants from varying calendar periods across five countries.
source: A total of nine cross-sectional studies reported breast cancer screening participation rates and represented >46,257,402 participants from varying calendar periods across five countries (Amornsiripanitch et al., 2021; Dennis et al., 2021; Fedewa et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021; NHS England, 2021; Campbell et al., 2021; Bessa, 2021; BreastScreen Aoteroa, 2022; Jidkova et al., 2022).

claim: Change in screening participation rates ranged from +2–8% in Scotland to –43.54% in Brazil.
source: There was considerable variability in change (Table 3), ranging from +2–8% in Scotland to –43.54% in Brazil (Campbell et al., 2021; Bessa, 2021).
evidence: Range of data with citations and reference to Table 3

claim: In the USA, there was a consistent negative change in screening participation uptake rates.
source: In the USA, there was a consistent negative change in screening participation uptake rates (Amornsiripanitch et al., 2021; Dennis et al., 2021; Fedewa et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021).

claim: 25 studies had no issues defining the inclusion sample.
source: From Table 4, 25 studies had no issues defining the inclusion sample.
evidence: Count from quality assessment in Table 4

claim: 19 studies were clear in defining the study setting and subjects.
source: Nineteen studies were clear in defining the study setting and subjects.

claim: All studies apart from Becker et al., 2021 had no issue measuring the condition through either screening appointment attendance or insurance claims data.
source: All studies apart from Becker et al., 2021 had no issue measuring the condition through either screening appointment attendance or insurance claims data.

claim: Most studies (65%, N = 17) did not define confounding factors regarding measurement of primary outcomes.
source: Most studies (65%, N = 17) did not define confounding factors regarding measurement of primary outcomes.
evidence: Quality assessment finding with percentage and count

claim: Twenty-three studies failed to provide strategies to address confounding factors.
source: Twenty-three studies failed to provide strategies to address confounding factors (e.g., elucidating reduction in capacity and presenting it as a proportion to overall volume).

claim: During COVID-19 there was a generally reported reduction in breast cancer screening volume and participation uptake rate that varied by healthcare setting.
source: In this rapid review, we show that during COVID-19 there was a generally reported reduction in breast cancer screening volume and participation uptake rate that varied by healthcare setting (e.g., national population-based screening vs. opportunistic or private healthcare).
evidence: Summary conclusion based on data from all included studies

claim: Volume and participation uptake are important metrics that requires monitoring by health systems and could inform prevention and early diagnosis efforts.
source: Our data suggests that volume and participation uptake are important metrics that requires monitoring by health systems and could inform prevention and early diagnosis efforts, especially if certain groups are not participating.

claim: Non-pharmaceutical interventions were essential and effective in containing the spread of COVID-19 in the era without vaccines.
source: Non-pharmaceutical interventions were essential and effective in containing the spread of COVID-19 in the era without vaccines; these extend to domestic/international movement controls, social distancing, and ban on events and gatherings and workplace/school closure (Li et al., 2021; Talic et al., 2021).

claim: A meta-analysis pooled an estimate from eight studies and indicated that handwashing (Relative Risk (RR): 0.47; 95% CI: 0.19–1.12), mask-wearing (RR: 0.47; 95% CI: 0.29–0.75), and physical distancing (RR: 0.75; 95% CI: 0.59–0.95) were associated with the reduction in COVID-19 incidence.
source: The meta-analysis pooled an estimate from eight studies and indicated that handwashing (Relative Risk (RR): 0.47; 95% CI: 0.19–1.12), mask-wearing (RR: 0.47; 95% CI: 0.29–0.75), and physical distancing (RR: 0.75; 95% CI: 0.59–0.95) were associated with the reduction in COVID-19 incidence.

claim: Reductions in screening capacity due to physical distancing are likely another source for screening volume reductions.
source: Reductions in screening capacity due to physical distancing are likely another source for screening volume reductions.
evidence: Inference based on understanding of healthcare operations during pandemic

claim: Screening capacity reductions were caused by social distancing, staggered appointments, staff exposure to COVID-19, and cleaning measures.
source: Screening capacity reductions were caused by social distancing, staggered appointments, staff exposure to COVID-19, and cleaning measures.
evidence: Inference based on pandemic healthcare practices

claim: Even though screening capacity recovered to pre-pandemic levels in July 2020, screening volume experienced a 10.8% decrease relative to the control period according to Sprague et al., 2021.
source: Even though screening capacity recovered to pre-pandemic levels in July 2020, screening volume experienced a 10.8% decrease relative to the control period.

claim: Most publications included in the rapid review did not collect data regarding screening capacity.
source: However, most publications included in our rapid review did not collect data regarding screening capacity, so we cannot determine the proportion of change in screening volume that was attributed to either reduction in screening capacity or change in patient willingness to attend screening.

claim: Data from the USA supports differences in screening volume changes by healthcare system.
source: Our data supports differences by healthcare system that were particularly evident in data from the USA where there is a mix of private and national healthcare (Medicare) for persons 65+ [https://www.medicare.gov/].
evidence: Inference from data patterns across studies

claim: DeGroff et al., 2021, who studied populations reliant solely on national health insurance, showed larger screening volume reductions (–39.00%).
source: DeGroff et al., 2021, who studied populations reliant solely on national health insurance, showed larger screening volume reductions (–39.00%).

claim: Medicaid and Medicare patients had –17.06% screening volume reduction compared to –10.50% experienced by the entire population according to Amornsiripanitch et al., 2021.
source: Medicaid and Medicare patients had –17.06% screening volume reduction compared to –10.50% experienced by the entire population.
evidence: Specific data comparison from cited study

claim: Miller et al., 2021 suggest that opportunity cost of attending breast screening in lower income groups (e.g., employment) may have led to decreased breast screening in such populations.
source: Miller et al., 2021 suggest that opportunity cost of attending breast screening in lower income groups (e.g., employment) may have led to decreased breast screening in such populations.

claim: The Affordable Care Act may have alleviated breast screening cost through health insurance coverage reforms.
source: The Affordable Care Act may have alleviated breast screening cost through health insurance coverage reforms (Zhao et al., 2020).

claim: Becker et al., 2021 showed a screening volume increase after the lifting of COVID-19 suspension guidelines.
source: Becker et al., 2021 showed a screening volume increase after the lifting of COVID-19 suspension guidelines.

claim: Campbell et al., 2021 state a 10.96% increase in uptake rate in Scotland.
source: Campbell et al., 2021 state a 10.96% increase in uptake rate in Scotland.

claim: The study population in Campbell et al., 2021 solely included patients who had their appointments cancelled in March 2020 due to the first lockdown and high-risk patients.
source: This study population (within the study period) solely included patients who had their appointments cancelled in March 2020 due to the first lockdown and high-risk patients.
evidence: Description of study population from cited study

claim: COVID-19 context is an evolving field with fast publication turnovers.
source: Other limitations include COVID-19 context as an evolving field with fast publication turnovers; more papers could have been published since the review started.

claim: Studies had insufficient data for combined analysis regarding COVID-19 waves past December 2020.
source: Other limitations included studies had insufficient data for combined analysis regarding COVID-19 waves past December 2020.

claim: The data obtained was cross-sectional instead of cohort-based.
source: Additionally, the data obtained was cross-sectional instead of cohort-based; we were unable to analyze trends and recovery in breast cancer screening rates and incidence rates over time.

claim: Exclusion of non-English-language literature was a weakness.
source: Exclusion of non-English-language literature was a weakness.

claim: Screening volume and uptake rates were generally reduced but many studies showed gains over time even if overall a decline in screening volume was observed.
source: In summary, screening volume and uptake rates were generally reduced but many studies showed gains over time even if overall a decline in screening volume was observed.
evidence: Summary of findings from all included studies

claim: Volume and uptake reductions of smaller magnitudes were observed, and data suggest some difference depending on region and healthcare coverage.
source: Volume and uptake reductions of smaller magnitudes were observed, and our data suggest some difference depending on region and healthcare coverage.

claim: Access to screening services may increase marginalization of some vulnerable groups in the USA due to the pandemic.
source: Access to screening services may increase marginalization of some vulnerable groups in the USA due to the pandemic

claim: Participation uptake and volume are not conclusive endpoints themselves.
source: Participation uptake and volume are not conclusive endpoints themselves, and future work from registries and other data sources are needed to determine whether there has been any impact on incidence, stage, and mortality outcomes.

claim: A systematic search was run on 'Ovid MEDLINE(R) and In-Process, In-Data-Review & Other Non-Indexed Citations' Database and WHO COVID-19 Literature Database, with entry date limits from January 1, 2020, to March 12, 2022.
source: RL ran a systematic search on 'Ovid MEDLINE(R) and In-Process, In-Data-Review & Other Non-Indexed Citations' Database and WHO COVID-19 Literature Database, with entry date limits from January 1, 2020, to March 12, 2022.

claim: Gray literature was searched from government health websites known to have data from population-based screening programs.
source: We searched gray literature from government health websites known to have data from population-based screening programs. These consisted of the National Cancer Institute (USA), CDC (USA), NHS (National Healthcare Service) UK database, BreastScreen Australia, and BreastScreen Aotearoa New Zealand.

claim: An English-language restriction was placed on the searches.
source: An English-language restriction was placed on the searches.

claim: All studies included had cross-sectional designs.
source: All studies included had cross-sectional designs.

claim: The JBI Critical Appraisal Tool for cross-sectional studies was used to assess the risk of bias of each article.
source: We used the JBI Critical Appraisal Tool for cross-sectional studies to assess the risk of bias of each article (Critical appraisal tools, 2022).
evidence: Description of quality assessment methodology with citation

claim: Data were synthesized descriptively since a meta-analysis was not appropriate due to heterogeneity of data.
source: Data were synthesized descriptively since a meta-analysis was not appropriate due to heterogeneity of data.

claim: Data was collected by comparing outcome measures before and after COVID-19 infection control measures were introduced.
source: Data was collected by comparing outcome measures before and after COVID-19 infection control measures were introduced; this was presumed due to the worldwide prevalence of COVID-19 by March 2020.

claim: Changes in screening participation volume in five nations with national population-based screening ranged from –13 to –31%.
source: Changes in screening participation volume in five nations with national population-based screening ranged from –13 to –31%.

claim: Among two countries with limited population-based programs, the decline in screening volume ranged from –61 to –41%.
source: Among two countries with limited population-based programs, the decline ranged from –61 to –41%.

claim: Within the USA, population participation volumes varied ranging from +18 to –39%.
source: Within the USA, population participation volumes varied ranging from +18 to –39%, with suggestion of differences by insurance status (HMO, Medicare, and low-income programs).

claim: Almost all studies had high risk of bias due to insufficient statistical analysis and confounding factors.
source: Almost all studies had high risk of bias due to insufficient statistical analysis and confounding factors.
evidence: Summary of quality assessment from abstract

claim: Reductions in screening volume and uptake rates were observed among eight countries.
source: Reductions in screening volume and uptake rates were observed among eight countries.

claim: The extent of COVID-19-induced reduction in breast screening participation volume differed by region.
source: The extent of COVID-19-induced reduction in breast screening participation volume differed by region and data suggested potential differences by healthcare setting (e.g., national health insurance vs. private healthcare).

claim: Data suggested potential differences in screening volume reduction by healthcare setting (e.g., national health insurance vs. private healthcare).
source: The extent of COVID-19-induced reduction in breast screening participation volume differed by region and data suggested potential differences by healthcare setting (e.g., national health insurance vs. private healthcare).

claim: Mammography-based screening programs allow for early detection of breast cancers for earlier intervention and disease stage that improves patient outcomes.
source: Mammography-based screening programs allow for early detection of breast cancers for earlier intervention and disease stage that improves patient outcomes (IARC, 2022).

claim: COVID-19 affected global health systems and has strained population breast mammography screening programs.
source: COVID-19 affected global health systems and has strained population breast mammography screening programs.
evidence: General statement based on pandemic impact

claim: In different countries, screening models vary from population-based to opportunistic screening.
source: In different countries, screening models vary from population-based to opportunistic screening (offered to patients in healthcare settings – more common in private healthcare) (IARC, 2016).

claim: Scotland and England were counted as two separate national entities due to the devolved healthcare systems.
source: We counted Scotland and England as two separate national entities due to the devolved healthcare systems.

claim: Breast screening policies and practice between NHS Scotland and NHS England are similar.
source: However, it should be noted that breast screening policies and practice between NHS Scotland and NHS England are similar.

claim: Most studies that showed calendar period trends of screening volume noted temporal variation with declines especially at the height of the pandemic between March and May 2020.
source: Most studies that showed calendar period trends of screening volume noted temporal variation with declines especially at the height of the pandemic between March and May 2020.
evidence: Summary of temporal patterns from multiple studies
